subject: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
parts:
I had an idea this morning for dealing with variability in detectability (or detectability components) for ecological models in general. I am wondering if anyone else has tried this or has any thoughts on its value. Also, please let me know if there are any existing posts on this approach.

In situations where we are primarily interested in ecological parameters (e.g., abundance, occupancy) and their covariate relationships, and we want to account for spatiotemporal variability in detectability, the two typical approaches are to specify some sort of random effect, include covariates on detectability, or both. Random effects are nice because they can reflect the sampling design and account for lots of different sources of variation, including those that the researcher has not thought of explicitly, but they are computationally expensive. Covariates are nice because they are computationally less expensive and can account for particular sources of variation thought to affect detectability, but the researcher may not have measured all important sources of variation in the form of a covariate.

I am wondering if it could be beneficial and relatively efficient to specify a latent covariate on detectability. I imagine that a latent covariate could account for major axes / sources of variation, including both spatial and temporal sources that have not been explicitly measured in the field, while being less costly in terms of computation and degrees of freedom than random effects.

Does anyone have any thoughts on the potential merits of specifying a latent covariate on detectability (or components of detectability) in terms of both efficacy and computational efficiency? Alternatively or additionally, can you suggest some sources that could provide insight on the merits of trying this out?

messages.author: ea29cead5e3b8075
messages.subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
parts:
Hi Quresh,

I think this ultimately depends on what you mean by a latent covariate. Are you referring to a latent 'grouping' variable (i.e., a finite mixture), where the user allows the model to assign individuals to some finite number of unobservable groups, where those groups would align with the most consistent among-individual similarities of heterogeneity in the data (which could be process or observation variation)? If so, these finite-mixtures have been used to a certain extent in the observational process in the past, but it's definitely not the most widespread type of model used in the mark-recapture field. That being said, the nimble folks and Oliver Gimenez have a recent paper that explores how these finite observational mixture models compare with a non-parametric approach to dealing with heterogeneity in the observational process (i.e., 'broken-stick' models), which is a more readily available model when using nimble. They provide code for each of the different model types. The finite-mixture models can be readily incorporated into JAGS models, but the broken-stick models may require a switch to nimble.

Turek et al. Bayesian non-parametric detection heterogeneity in ecological models. link: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10651-021-00489-1

Although I really like Turek's paper and the model itself, I am not certain that it is computationally more efficient than a random effects model. I think some of the authors are on this listserv, so they may be able to chime in with more insights.


-Dan

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
parts:
Dear Dan, Quresh,

interesting discussion. I think that such latent variables have a wide scope of application in stats. For instance, they have been used by people modeling pair-wise correlations in species occurrence in communities. The TREE paper by Warton et al. gives a nice explanation in their Box 1: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169534715002402
So Many Variables: Joint Modeling in Community Ecology - ScienceDirect
Technological advances have enabled a new class of multivariate models for ecology, with the potential now to specify a statistical model for abundances jointly across many taxa, to simultaneously explore interactions across taxa and the response of abundance to environmental variables.
www.sciencedirect.com

It sounds like magic: you estimate not only a coefficient of a covariate, but also the covariate values alongside.

I don't have any intuition about whether this construct could be useful for modeling detection heterogeneity, so my usual answer would then be "Simulation is the answer". Perhaps you can simulate a couple of data sets with different patterns in detection probability (specified for instance by covariates and/or random effects), then ignore that info and see whether and how well you can recover part of it using such latent variables ?

Best regards  -- Marc

parts: Adding my conversation with Thomas Riecke to this thread in case anyone may benefit (minus a pre-publication MS).

Quresh S. Latif 
Research Scientist
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15

From: Thomas Riecke <thomasva...@gmail.com>
Sent: Friday, January 21, 2022 3:53 PM
To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
Subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?

Hi Quresh,

 

First, I should've mentioned the Duarte, Link, and Barker (all et al. 2018) papers earlier, they talk quite a bit about similar issues. These models (random effects on p) are pretty much intrinsically not identifiable. I'll try not to go too far down the rabbit hole of what I think about that, but your definition sounds excellent to me!

 

Regarding fixing the sign, yea, but it's a little bit more complicated than that. I attached a script with some comments. A key thing to note is that you have to either fix the variance of a latent covariate (and the sign of the effect), or fix the effect of a latent covariate. Otherwise the variance and effect perfectly covary (and can covary a bit with the intercept). In the simulation we just fix N so that the variance in p is identifiable.

 

So if we assume some observation model (ignoring subscripts):

y ~ binomial(N, p)

 

here is a random effect model for p:

epsilon ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + epsilon

 

Here is a latent covariate model with a fixed effect for p:

eta ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + theta * eta

theta = 1

 

Those are the same models? I think if you fix the variance you're just re-scaling the covariate (i.e., also the same thing). I attached a very rough draft of a manuscript where we use a latent variable for multiple observed processes (hatch date and prey captures), and then use it as a covariate for different demographic parameters, and there are some other examples in the script that really delve into why some of those problems occur.

 

Finally (if you're still reading!), Dan (who responded earlier) and I recently published a paper with Marc and Michael where we do something kind of similar to what you're suggesting. We include a random effect for every survey, but we include multiple species in the analysis, and the random effect is shared across species. So the assumption is that whatever weird combination of date, time, observer, local weather is affecting one species affects all of them in the same way around their various species-specific detection intercepts. This could be structured in a SEM kind of approach as well, and I think it's identifiable, but of course if our assumptions about the structure of heterogeneity are incorrect then it will return poor parameter estimates. Link here:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/ece3.8410

 

Thomas

 

On Fri, Jan 21, 2022 at 9:15 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

I think I just realized why you might think there might be identifiability issues! If we don’t specify a priori the sign of the regression parameter, then indeed the model would not be identifiable. I restricted the prior for the regression parameter to be positive, which I think makes it identifiable. I think this is analogous to restricting group k to always have a larger parameter estimate than group k-1 in finite-mixture models.

Quresh S. Latif 
Research Scientist
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15
www.birdconservancy.org

 

From: Thomas Riecke <thomasva...@gmail.com>
Sent: Friday, January 21, 2022 10:46 AM
To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
Subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?

 

Hi Quresh,

I’m traveling with my girlfriend right now. I can shoot you some code later. I think there will be very strong covariance between the posterior for variance of the latent covariate and the posterior for the regression parameter. The chains might converge, but that doesn’t necessarily imply identifiability.

 

Anyway, I could totally be wrong :) I’ll shoot ya some code this evening and then we’ll have something to talk about that’s more clearly defined?

 

Thomas

 

On Fri, Jan 21, 2022 at 09:36 Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

Thanks! In a different context, I was able to get a model estimating an intercept, a latent variable, and the regression parameter to converge (Rhats all ~1). Exploration of the posterior estimates suggested the model was doing what I had intended – i.e., estimate latent variable value while also estimating the dependent variable’s relationship with those values. Seems like that means the model is identifiable, right, or am I missing something? I think conceptually it is analogous to multivariate statistical approaches like canonical correlation analysis or PCA, which also in one way or another, quantify latent variables representing major axes of variation in the data.

 

I’ll look up that reference, thanks! Also, I had not connected this idea to structural equation modeling, and I don’t have much experience with those beyond whatever material came up in stats classes in grad school, so thanks for that lead. Makes sense that SEM would involve modeling latent variables. I’ll have to think about that connection more.

Quresh S. Latif 
Research Scientist
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15
www.birdconservancy.org

 

From: Thomas Riecke <thomasva...@gmail.com>
Sent: Friday, January 21, 2022 10:25 AM
To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
Subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?

As a quick follow up, the ‘blavaan’ package can be very helpful for outputting SEMs and path analyses into JAGS or Stan model code.

 

On Fri, Jan 21, 2022 at 09:11 Thomas Riecke <thomasva...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Quresh,

 

There are identifiability constraints with the use of latent variables. So I don’t think you could simultaneously estimate the variance of a latent variable, an intercept and a regression parameter. Cubaynes et al is a good paper about latent variables in a cmr framework. Pearl has tons of great work on SEMs and latent variables. Lots of other good stuff out there.

 

I may not fully understand your question, but I guess given identifiability constraints there is no difference between a random effect and an unobserved latent covariate?

 

Thomas

Hi Quresh,

 

First, I should've mentioned the Duarte, Link, and Barker (all et al. 2018) papers earlier, they talk quite a bit about similar issues. These models (random effects on p) are pretty much intrinsically not identifiable. I'll try not to go too far down the rabbit hole of what I think about that, but your definition sounds excellent to me!

 

Regarding fixing the sign, yea, but it's a little bit more complicated than that. I attached a script with some comments. A key thing to note is that you have to either fix the variance of a latent covariate (and the sign of the effect), or fix the effect of a latent covariate. Otherwise the variance and effect perfectly covary (and can covary a bit with the intercept). In the simulation we just fix N so that the variance in p is identifiable.

 

So if we assume some observation model (ignoring subscripts):

y ~ binomial(N, p)

 

here is a random effect model for p:

epsilon ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + epsilon

 

Here is a latent covariate model with a fixed effect for p:

eta ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + theta * eta

theta = 1

 

Those are the same models? I think if you fix the variance you're just re-scaling the covariate (i.e., also the same thing). I attached a very rough draft of a manuscript where we use a latent variable for multiple observed processes (hatch date and prey captures), and then use it as a covariate for different demographic parameters, and there are some other examples in the script that really delve into why some of those problems occur.

 

Finally (if you're still reading!), Dan (who responded earlier) and I recently published a paper with Marc and Michael where we do something kind of similar to what you're suggesting. We include a random effect for every survey, but we include multiple species in the analysis, and the random effect is shared across species. So the assumption is that whatever weird combination of date, time, observer, local weather is affecting one species affects all of them in the same way around their various species-specific detection intercepts. This could be structured in a SEM kind of approach as well, and I think it's identifiable, but of course if our assumptions about the structure of heterogeneity are incorrect then it will return poor parameter estimates. Link here:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/ece3.8410

 

Thomas

Hi Quresh,

 

I think this ultimately depends on what you mean by a latent covariate. Are you referring to a latent 'grouping' variable (i.e., a finite mixture), where the user allows the model to assign individuals to some finite number of unobservable groups, where those groups would align with the most consistent among-individual similarities of heterogeneity in the data (which could be process or observation variation)? If so, these finite-mixtures have been used to a certain extent in the observational process in the past, but it's definitely not the most widespread type of model used in the mark-recapture field. That being said, the nimble folks and Oliver Gimenez have a recent paper that explores how these finite observational mixture models compare with a non-parametric approach to dealing with heterogeneity in the observational process (i.e., 'broken-stick' models), which is a more readily available model when using nimble. They provide code for each of the different model types. The finite-mixture models can be readily incorporated into JAGS models, but the broken-stick models may require a switch to nimble.

 

Turek et al. Bayesian non-parametric detection heterogeneity in ecological models. link: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10651-021-00489-1

 

Although I really like Turek's paper and the model itself, I am not certain that it is computationally more efficient than a random effects model. I think some of the authors are on this listserv, so they may be able to chime in with more insights.

 

 

-Dan

 

 

 

On Fri, Jan 21, 2022 at 9:07 AM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

I had an idea this morning for dealing with variability in detectability (or detectability components) for ecological models in general. I am wondering if anyone else has tried this or has any thoughts on its value. Also, please let me know if there are any existing posts on this approach.

 

In situations where we are primarily interested in ecological parameters (e.g., abundance, occupancy) and their covariate relationships, and we want to account for spatiotemporal variability in detectability, the two typical approaches are to specify some sort of random effect, include covariates on detectability, or both. Random effects are nice because they can reflect the sampling design and account for lots of different sources of variation, including those that the researcher has not thought of explicitly, but they are computationally expensive. Covariates are nice because they are computationally less expensive and can account for particular sources of variation thought to affect detectability, but the researcher may not have measured all important sources of variation in the form of a covariate.

 

I am wondering if it could be beneficial and relatively efficient to specify a latent covariate on detectability. I imagine that a latent covariate could account for major axes / sources of variation, including both spatial and temporal sources that have not been explicitly measured in the field, while being less costly in terms of computation and degrees of freedom than random effects.

 

Does anyone have any thoughts on the potential merits of specifying a latent covariate on detectability (or components of detectability) in terms of both efficacy and computational efficiency? Alternatively or additionally, can you suggest some sources that could provide insight on the merits of trying this out?

Hi Quresh,

This is something I've also been interested in and messing around with for a few different multi-species applications where spatial/spatiotemporal variation in the sampling effort within a given site is known or suspected, with good reason to believe all species will not respond the same and some interest in inter-specific detection correlation (sensu some of the papers previously mentioned).  Not sure if this mirrors your motivation and I've not explored modeling decisions (a la Tobler et al. 2019 in Ecology) in any depth, but certainly seem to be benefits associated with dimension reduction relative to random effects for each individual species (structured by site or site*survey). 

If this is the sort of thing you were thinking of, just wanted to note that there seem to be mixed schools of thought regarding whether loadings/coefficients should be constrained within the sampling process (certain loadings forced to be positive, whatever) vs. aligned/transformed after the fact. My limited understanding is that the latter tactic is more efficient (blaavan employs it, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07733.pdf).

Cheers,

John
